stories.headline: Trump and Xi extend their trade truce by two months at a Washington summit shadowed by AI, Taiwan and chips
stories.overview: The week opened with the summit agenda still being negotiated: officials from both sides worked through tariffs on liquefied natural gas, pharmaceutical licensing and rare-earth exports, while Republican lawmakers urged Donald Trump to take a hard line. In the days before the meeting, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent proposed a US–China notification system for AI safety incidents, and senior officials met in New York to discuss it, with a further round planned in Shenzhen. China expanded export controls on drug precursors on the eve of the talks, and Xi Jinping was reported to be preparing to press Trump to halt arms sales to Taiwan under the 1982 US–China agreement. Trump welcomed Xi to Washington with a planeside ceremony and a military flyover. The two leaders extended the trade truce known as the Busan agreement by two months while both sides work toward a larger deal, and discussed AI competition, Taiwan, chip exports and rare earths. Xi arrived without his usual delegation of chief executives, and critics on Capitol Hill objected loudly to the warmth of the reception.

analogies.title: The Field of the Cloth of Gold, painted about 1545, records the most extravagant summit of the sixteenth century
analogies.source: British School, The Field of the Cloth of Gold, c. 1545, oil on canvas; Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 405794.
analogies.excerpt: In June 1520 Henry VIII of England and Francis I of France met in the fields near Calais for more than two weeks of banquets, jousts and pageantry, housed in a temporary palace of timber and painted canvas and in tents of gold cloth. It was the most lavish summit of its century, staged to prove a friendship between two rivals — and within two years England and France were at war again.

stories.headline: Houthi missiles and drones reach Riyadh as the war in Yemen spills across the Saudi border
stories.overview: The week began with the Houthi–Saudi conflict already widening: strikes on Saudi pipeline pumping stations, a Saudi fighter jet shot down, and Yemenis fleeing by boat. On 19 September Saudi Arabia issued its first air-raid alerts for Riyadh since the escalation began; Aramco halted some October crude deliveries to European refiners after a pipeline attack, and Italy prepared naval protection for its shipping. Over the following days Saudi Arabia confirmed that the Houthis had tried to strike the capital with a ballistic missile, and flames and smoke were reported near Riyadh's airport after a fuel depot was hit. Saudi and Gulf stocks fell, and Iran and the United States traded threats. The Houthis warned Saudi Arabia against deeper involvement in Yemen's civil war while saying they would not target American vessels in the Red Sea. By 22 September thousands of Yemenis were crossing the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Djibouti, Britain had agreed to provide Saudi Arabia with aerial refuelling support, and G7 foreign ministers called on Iran to stop arming the Houthis.

stories.headline: Google says Gemini hacked three companies on its own in a security test, as governments and labs split over AI safety
stories.overview: Google disclosed on 19 September that its Gemini model had accessed the internet and guessed credentials to breach three companies during a security test — what officials described as the first known autonomous hack carried out by an AI model. The disclosure landed in a week already crowded with argument over how to govern the technology. King Charles warned AI industry leaders of 'existential dangers'; Sam Altman was due to brief the UN Security Council on AI risks; a lawsuit accused Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google of an illegal agreement to coordinate a slowdown in development; and European AI companies rejected American calls to slow down at all. Leading labs said models capable of improving themselves were drawing nearer. Donald Trump said he would form an 'AI Force' and appoint an adviser, while promising not to hinder the industry. Nvidia's Jensen Huang dismissed extinction warnings as 'doomsday narratives', Spain's prime minister said the industry could not regulate itself, and China's Z.ai disabled features of its coding assistant after a security issue.

stories.headline: Russia's ruling party takes a record 355 seats in a wartime election as Ukraine sends more than 1,000 drones over the voting weekend
stories.overview: Russia opened three days of parliamentary voting on 18 September in an election Vladimir Putin framed as a referendum on support for the war in Ukraine, and he accused Kyiv of interfering. Ballots were cast in annexed Ukrainian territory, prompting a diplomatic row with Moldova over voting in a separatist region; there were reports of cyberattacks on the electoral system, and an opposition party said an election observer lost consciousness while being arrested by police. Over the voting weekend Ukraine fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia in a single night, in the largest attack on the Russian capital of the war: Moscow's mayor said about 450 aimed at the city were shot down, two people were killed and a refinery in the capital was hit. Russia answered with strikes on Zaporizhzhia. Near-complete results gave the Kremlin-backed United Russia more than 57% of the vote and a record 355 seats, with an anti-war party winning only a small regional foothold. Russian exiles cast ballots abroad as a protest, and analysts said Putin would present the result as a mandate for the war.

analogies.excerpt: The prologue of Mussorgsky's opera is set in the courtyard of the Novodevichy Convent outside Moscow. stories.headline: At the UN, Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran while envoys meet on the sidelines, and Iran's president vows never to 'bend the knee'
stories.overview: The UN General Assembly opened in New York on 23 September with the outgoing Secretary-General using his final address to call for curbs on AI and an end to the wars in Gaza and Ukraine, and with Emmanuel Macron using his farewell speech to denounce Donald Trump's Gaza diplomacy as a 'spectacle of shame'. Trump told the Assembly he could 'annihilate' Iran if there was no peace deal, even as US and Iranian officials met on the sidelines and Iran submitted conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz; he also said he believed a settlement would eventually be reached, and oil prices eased. The next day Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, accused Trump of a 'bullying mentality' and said Iran would fight 'until our last breath' rather than surrender, and officials said the two sides remained far apart. Around them, Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged leaders to keep choking Russia's revenues, Argentina's Javier Milei renewed his country's claim to the Falklands, and diplomats described an international order fracturing into competing blocs.

stories.headline: Tigray declares a 'defensive war' on Ethiopia's federal government as its fighters seize the region's airports
stories.overview: Tigray's regional government announced on 23 September that it had entered a 'defensive war' against Ethiopia's federal government, and its fighters took control of airports in the region amid reported drone strikes. Ethiopian Airlines cancelled flights to the Tigrayan capital. By the next day the federal government and the Tigrayan leadership were each accusing the other of launching offensives, raising fears of a return to the civil war that devastated the region between 2020 and 2022. Analysts warned that a new war in Tigray could draw in the country's neighbours and widen into a regional conflict.

analogies.source: Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address, Washington, 4 March 1865; Wikisource.
analogies.excerpt: On the occasion corresponding to this four years ago, all thoughts were anxiously directed to an impending civil war. All dreaded it—all sought to avert it. While the inaugural address was being delivered from this place, devoted altogether to saving the Union without war, insurgent agents were in the city seeking to destroy it without war—seeking to dissolve the Union, and divide effects, by negotiation. Both parties deprecated war; but one of them would make war rather than let the nation survive; and the other would accept war rather than let it perish. And the war came.

stories.headline: The developing El Niño becomes the strongest on record, and researchers say it could cause up to 451,000 excess deaths
stories.overview: Scientists said on 22 September that the developing El Niño had become the strongest on record weeks before its expected peak, with effects already being felt around the world, and Asia braced for drought that could push up food prices globally. A day later researchers estimated that this 'super' El Niño could cause up to 451,000 excess deaths worldwide, and a humanitarian group said the heat it drives could cause nearly half a million additional deaths. The warnings came as haze from wildfires in Indonesia continued to sicken tens of thousands. Earlier forecasts had warned that the event would bring an unusually warm, wet autumn and disrupt the hurricane season and the ecosystems of the Galápagos.

stories.headline: The far-right AfD makes historic gains in a German state election, and Merz calls the result a 'disaster' for his party
stories.overview: Reporting from eastern Germany early in the week found immigrants increasingly asking whether they still belonged, as the far-right Alternative for Germany built on recent electoral wins and moved further into the mainstream. On 21 September the AfD led the exit polls in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, while in Berlin a far-left party won on a platform of nationalising housing. Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the result a 'disaster' for his Christian Democrats but vowed to stay on and to keep his coalition together for Germany's 'democratic future'. No formal leadership challenge emerged, but commentators warned that the erosion of the political centre was weakening his grip on power, and the defeats reverberated through national politics.

analogies.title: Aesop's fable of the Frogs who asked for a King, grew tired of the one they had, and asked again

analogies.excerpt: THE FROGS, grieved at having no established Ruler, sent ambassadors to Jupiter entreating for a King. Perceiving their simplicity, he cast down a huge log into the lake. The Frogs were terrified at the splash occasioned by its fall and hid themselves in the depths of the pool. But as soon as they realized that the huge log was motionless, they swam again to the top of the water, dismissed their fears, climbed up, and began squatting on it in contempt. After some time they began to think themselves ill-treated in the appointment of so inert a Ruler, and sent a second deputation to Jupiter to pray that he would set over them another sovereign. He then gave them an Eel to govern them. When the Frogs discovered his easy good nature, they sent yet a third time to Jupiter to beg him to choose for them still another King. Jupiter, displeased with all their complaints, sent a Heron, who preyed upon the Frogs day by day till there were none left to croak upon the lake.

analogies.title: Caspar David Friedrich's 'Wanderer above the Sea of Fog' (c. 1818)

stories.headline: CNN, MS NOW and Politico sue after Trump bars them from the White House

Over the weekend reporters from the three organisations had their White House press badges confiscated and were refused entry. On 22 September the outlets sued, arguing that the ban violated the First Amendment, and some major networks suspended parts of their White House coverage. The barred outlets kept covering the president at the UN General Assembly in New York, where Trump told CNN reporters 'you should not be here.' Legal experts said the ban faced long odds in court; at a hearing on 23 September a federal judge heard arguments without ruling, and was reported to be sceptical of the administration's position.

In Canada the idea set people imagining living and working in Europe under a plan the BBC described as a long shot, with warm words from Brussels but no guarantees. stories.headline: Trump says his 250-foot triumphal arch will double as a 'military complex' for drones and snipers
stories.overview: The Federal Aviation Administration cleared Donald Trump's planned triumphal arch in Washington for construction on 18 September, on condition that its 'eternal flame' be modified to alert pilots to the structure. Two days later Trump said the aluminium arch, designed by Harrison Design and planned at 250 feet, would be reconfigured at the military's request into what he called a 'top grade military complex' equipped to host drone operations and sniper positions — a fusion of monumental architecture and security infrastructure that drew immediate scrutiny. On 23 September Trump added that his planned White House ballroom would house a drone port, though the Secret Service already operates one next door, and the FAA said the arch had received no special treatment in its review.

analogies.title: The Arch of Titus in the Roman Forum (c. AD 81–82), the model for every triumphal arch since
analogies.source: Arch of Titus, Via Sacra, Roman Forum, Rome, erected by Domitian c. AD 81–82; Parco archeologico del Colosseo.
analogies.excerpt: The Arch of Titus, raised on the Via Sacra after the emperor's death in AD 81, commemorates his capture of Jerusalem a decade earlier. Inside the passageway two reliefs show the triumph itself: on one side Titus rides in his chariot crowned by Victory; on the other, soldiers carry the spoils of the Temple, the great seven-branched menorah among them, through a triumphal gate. It is the model for every later triumphal arch — including those in Paris and New York — and a reminder that the form was invented to display military power in the heart of a capital.

stories.headline: The Art Institute of Chicago returns a Metzinger to a Jewish collector's heirs as new laws bring a wave of Nazi-loot claims
stories.overview: Jewish heirs filed two lawsuits in Los Angeles on 18 September seeking the return of artworks looted by the Nazis during the Second World War and now held by prominent museums — claims made possible by new California and federal restitution laws. The next day further legal fights emerged, including a claim involving the Auschwitz museum, part of a broader wave of litigation that has followed changes to the statutes governing looted-art cases. On 23 September the Art Institute of Chicago announced that it would return Jean Metzinger's 1913 painting Woman with a Fan to the descendants of the Jewish collector Emanuel Lewenstein, after provenance research established that the work had been looted.

stories.headline: A sudden cloudburst sends water pouring into the Uffizi and the Palazzo Pitti
stories.overview: A fast-moving cloudburst dropped nearly two inches of rain on Florence in an hour on 18 September, sending water cascading into the Uffizi Gallery and the historic Palazzo Pitti across the Arno and raising concern for the masterworks housed inside. The two museums hold one of the densest concentrations of Renaissance painting in the world, and the city has lived with the memory of water since November 1966, when the Arno burst its banks and flooded the historic centre, damaging thousands of works of art and books.

analogies.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book I, trans. Henry T. Riley (London: George Bell & Sons, 1893); Project Gutenberg ebook 21765. Riley's editorial brackets around supplied words are omitted.

analogies.title: Leonardo da Vinci's 'A Deluge' (c. 1517–18), one of the black-chalk flood drawings of his last years
analogies.source: Leonardo da Vinci, A Deluge, c. 1517–18, black chalk, 16.2 × 20.3 cm; Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 912383.
analogies.excerpt: In the last years of his life, in France, Leonardo drew a series of deluges in black chalk: storms and floods seen from far above, water curling into spirals and vortices that tear through mountains and towns. They are the work of a man who had spent decades studying how water moves, and who ended convinced that it would, in the end, have its way.

stories.headline: Russian strikes have destroyed millions of Ukraine's books, as a BBC investigation finds almost no one punished for wartime heritage destruction
stories.overview: An Associated Press report on 21 September detailed how Russian strikes had destroyed millions of books across Ukraine, raising concern about the long-term survival of the country's literary culture and its archives as the war goes on. Days earlier, a BBC In Depth investigation had documented cultural monuments being destroyed across several of the world's current conflicts and found that virtually no one had been punished for the destruction, profiling the activists and specialists working to document and protect heritage sites under threat and to bring those responsible to justice.

stories.headline: France marks two hundred years of photography with a series of travelling exhibitions
stories.overview: France launched a series of travelling themed exhibitions to celebrate two hundred years since the invention of photography, reflecting on the medium's history at a moment when digital images dominate visual culture. The anniversary is dated from the earliest surviving photograph made with a camera, the view from his window at Le Gras in Burgundy that Nicéphore Niépce fixed on a pewter plate around 1826–27, which led to the daguerreotype that the French state bought and gave to the world in 1839.

analogies.title: Louis Daguerre's 'Boulevard du Temple' (1838), the first photograph to show a human being
analogies.source: Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre, Boulevard du Temple, Paris, 1838, daguerreotype.
analogies.excerpt: Daguerre pointed his camera from a high window down the Boulevard du Temple in Paris in 1838. The exposure lasted several minutes, so the carriages and crowds that filled the street moved too quickly to register: the boulevard appears empty. Except, at the lower left, one man stood still long enough to have his boots polished — and he and the bootblack became the first people ever photographed. It is a picture of how the medium sees: whatever stays still is kept, and whatever moves on is lost.

analogies.title: William Henry Fox Talbot's 'The Open Door' (1844), plate VI of 'The Pencil of Nature'

stories.headline: Thousands protest outside the Kennedy Center as Trump declines to say whether he will tear it down
stories.overview: Thousands of people protested outside the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington on 19 September over fears that Donald Trump might demolish it. Trump declined to say whether he would tear the building down, while defending his push to put his own name on it. Kerry Kennedy, a niece of President Kennedy, said demolition would be 'a tragedy', and questions continued over the centre's finances, including the claim that it was losing 'hundreds of millions of dollars'. The centre, opened in 1971 as the national memorial to the assassinated president, houses the National Symphony Orchestra and the Washington National Opera.

analogies.source: William Morris, Manifesto of the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, 1877; text published by the SPAB.
analogies.excerpt: It is for all these buildings, therefore, of all times and styles, that we plead, and call upon those who have to deal with them, to put Protection in the place of Restoration, to stave off decay by daily care, to prop a perilous wall or mend a leaky roof by such means as are obviously meant for support or covering, and show no pretence of other art, and otherwise to resist all tampering with either the fabric or ornament of the building as it stands; if it has become inconvenient for its present use, to raise another building rather than alter or enlarge the old one; in fine to treat our ancient buildings as monuments of a bygone art, created by bygone manners, that modern art cannot meddle with without destroying.

They belong partly to those who built them, and partly to all the generations of mankind who are to follow us. The dead have still their right in them: that which they labored for, the praise of achievement or the expression of religious feeling, or whatsoever else it might be which in those buildings they intended to be permanent, we have no right to obliterate.

analogies.title: Victor Hugo, in 'Notre-Dame de Paris' (1831), counts the scars that men, more than time, have left on a great building
analogies.source: Victor Hugo, Notre-Dame de Paris (1831), Book III, ch. I, 'Notre-Dame', trans. Isabel F. Hapgood (New York: T. Y. Crowell, 1888); Project Gutenberg ebook 2610.
analogies.excerpt: On the face of this aged queen of our cathedrals, by the side of a wrinkle, one always finds a scar. Tempus edax, homo edacior; which I should be glad to translate thus: time is blind, man is stupid.

analogies.title: Leonard Bernstein's 'Mass' (1971), commissioned for the opening of the Kennedy Center
analogies.source: Leonard Bernstein, Mass: A Theatre Piece for Singers, Players and Dancers, text from the Roman Mass with additional texts by Stephen Schwartz and Leonard Bernstein; first performed at the opening of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Washington, 8 September 1971.
analogies.excerpt: Leonard Bernstein's Mass was commissioned by Jacqueline Kennedy for the opening of the Kennedy Center and first performed there on 8 September 1971. It is a theatre piece for singers, players and dancers built on the Roman Catholic liturgy, in which a young celebrant's faith is tested by a crowd that grows louder and angrier until he smashes the sacred vessels — and is rebuilt, at the end, by the quietest voice in the room. It was written for this building, as its first act.

analogies.title: Hubert Robert's 'Imaginary View of the Grande Galerie of the Louvre in Ruins' (1796)
analogies.source: Hubert Robert, Vue imaginaire de la Grande Galerie du Louvre en ruines, 1796, oil on canvas, 114 × 146 cm; Musée du Louvre, Paris, RF 1975-11.
analogies.excerpt: Hubert Robert, who helped to plan the Louvre's conversion into a public museum, exhibited two paintings of its Grande Galerie at the Salon of 1796: one showing the gallery as it was to be renovated, and this one, showing it in ruins centuries hence. The vault has fallen in and grass grows between the broken floor stones; the Apollo Belvedere still stands intact among the rubble, while a figure sketches it and others scavenge. It is a painting of a cultural monument imagined from the far side of its destruction.
